title: Moonlight passback: metric-capture notes for Miguel Santos
content:
Quick context: Miguel Santos interviewed for Senior Runtime Engineer (inference-serving). He was the on-call candidate this week — short loop: 50m technical + 30m system design. This is my nightcap passback with metric-style signals (so we can compare to other candidates later).

Quick take: strong intuition for memory/kv-cache tradeoffs, pragmatic about quantization limits. Communication is terse but clear; sometimes jumps to low-level optimizations before making the high-level tradeoff explicit. Would slot well as a mid-to-senior infra engineer who can own a latency-critical surface after a short ramp.

Score breakdown (1-5, 5=excellent):
- Technical fundamentals: 4 — Good mastery of transformer execution flow, attention cache, and batching dynamics. Could articulate where CPU vs GPU bottlenecks show up for short vs long sequences.
- Systems design / architecture: 3.5 — Proposes solid designs (shard-by-request hashing, KV cache eviction TTLs), but less attention to operational failure modes (heartbeat, blackhole detection).
- Debugging / troubleshooting: 4.5 — Very fast at narrowing down memory blowups and demonstrating flamegraph reasoning; suggested clever use of memory pools and pinned allocator heuristics.
- Communication and collaboration: 3 — Direct, sometimes assumes interviewers are aligned on signal. Might need coaching to slow down for cross-team knowledge transfer.
- Product sense & tradeoffs: 3.5 — Understands cost/latency tradeoffs; defaulted to engineering-first choices rather than product-level safety nets (eg. circuit breakers, graceful degradation).

Notable strengths / signals:
- Live coding: wrote a small pseudo-allocator sketch that showed how to track per-request KV Cache usage and evict by recency-weighted token-cost. Clean, incremental approach.
- Latency thinking: called out tail latency vs median; proposed per-model async batching where small requests take a fast-path without waiting for a full batch — with hedging fallback to a slow-path batch.
- Cost-sensitivity: advocated for mixed-precision + per-customer quantization profiles and a runtime policy layer that picks quant level by customer SLA. Practical and likely to save ~$ on tokens.

Red flags / unanswered questions:
- Production ownership examples were light. Could not point to specific incidents where they led rollbacks/SEV triage. Need concrete postmortem artifact.
- Observability: suggested ad-hoc logs and flamegraphs but did not propose concrete tracing spans or dashboard KPIs (p95 token latency by model, per-tenant QPS).
- Cross-team collaboration: concerned about his tendency to PR small, iterative fixes directly; may need guidance for larger design docs and stakeholder alignment.

Behavioral notes (informal):
- Calm under pressure, asked good clarifying questions early in system design prompt.
- Uses domain shorthand a lot ("prefetch KV"/"flush hot cache") — good for fast engineering teams but could confuse product/CS partners.

Suggested follow-ups / interview plan:
- Ask for a 45m on-call postmortem walkthrough: request a concrete SEV postmortem he authored or co-authored. That will surface ownership and incident response depth.
- Have him pair with an SRE candidate or SRE interviewer on an observability exercise: design the tracing/spans/alerting/SLI/monitoring for an inference endpoint. Focus: show concrete dashboards and alert thresholds.
- Optional: small take-home to implement a simulated KV cache eviction policy (python) with metrics collection (p95, eviction rate) — can be used to evaluate coding clarity and telemetry thinking.

Suggested hiring recommendation (short): Strong technical base for runtime and inference optimizations. Recommend proceed to one deeper ops/ownership loop focused on incident response and monitoring. Not yet ready for a wide-scoped ownership role without evidence of SEV leadership.

Random notes to self / snippets to capture for the packet:
- Miguel emphasized "per-sequence affinity" when designing batch assignment — phrase to capture in packet.
- He referenced a "pinned allocator" pattern used at previous employer (ask for repo or code snippet).
- He proposed a rolling fallback: if lightweight path misses, reissue to batch and tag request with "hedge=true" — nice engineering pattern, add to interview score rationale.

Draft blurb for hiring packet (1-2 lines):
"Miguel Santos demonstrates solid execution knowledge for inference runtimes with practical cost-saving instincts (quantization + runtime policies). Recommend further evaluation on incident ownership and observability design before moving to offer."

Open asks for candidate:
1) Can he share a postmortem or incident timeline where his actions changed outcome?
2) Code sample (allocator / caching) to validate style and readability.
3) Example dashboards/alerts he has created (or at least a spec).

Action items (who/when):
- Jordan: request postmortem and code sample from Miguel (send follow-up email tonight).
- Maya: schedule observability pair loop if candidate shares artifacts (aim for next week).
- Evan: draft take-home spec if we decide to gate on code sample (2 day micro-project).

Bottom line: Good fit for a fast-moving infra team that needs hands-on runtime optimizations. Wants a short ops loop to validate production ownership. If artifacts check out, would champion for hire with manager-level mentorship on cross-team documentation and postmortem leadership.

End of passback.
